marsabit.title: Marsabit County
marsabit.gam: 18–26% (North Horr & Laisamis highest, recent SMART surveys)
marsabit.intro: Kenya's second-largest county and PACIDA's home base. A vast basalt-and-desert landscape running from the shores of Lake Turkana across the Chalbi Desert — Kenya's only true desert — to the Ethiopian border at Moyale. Mt. Marsabit's forested volcanic massif (1,700 m) is a green island whose mist-fed highlands support the county's only rain-fed agriculture; everything around it is camel, goat and small-stock country of the Gabra, Rendille, Borana, Burji, Turkana, Samburu, Dassanach and El Molo peoples. Annual rainfall spans 200 mm on the Chalbi floor to 800+ mm on the mountain. Poverty (83.2%) is among the highest in Kenya and 80% of livelihoods depend directly on livestock.
subcounties: Butiye, Somare, Odda, Uran, Golbo plains, Godoma
Karare, Sagante, Jaldesa, Dirib Gombo, Songa, Badassa, Kituruni
Dukana, Balesa, El Gade, Darade, Illeret, Malabot
Korr, Kargi, Ngurunit, Logologo, Merille, Ilaut
Maikona, Kalacha, Bubisa, Turbi, Hurri Hills, Forolle
Sololo Makutano, Ambalo, Dambala Fachana, Uran, Walda
El Molo Bay, Moite, Gatab (Mt Kulal), Arapal, Sarima, South Horr road
sectors: Livestock economy

≈80% of household income is livestock-based. Camels are the drought-critical species (milk through dry seasons); Merille and Moyale are the key livestock markets. 2019 census recorded well over 2 million goats and sheep, ~420,000 cattle and ~240,000 camels in the county (indicative).
Water & WASH

Household water is from boreholes, shallow wells (Chalbi springs at Kalacha/Maikona), pans and rock catchments. In drought, trekking distances exceed 15–25 km in North Horr and Laisamis; NDMA's Jan 2026 bulletin flagged Marsabit among counties with the longest grazing-to-water distances. Badassa dam and desalination pilots serve the highlands.
Nutrition & health

GAM has repeatedly breached the WHO 15% 'critical' emergency threshold in North Horr and Laisamis during droughts (SMART surveys 18–26%). PPR, CCPP and FMD livestock disease outbreaks were reported county-wide in early 2026, cutting milk availability for children.
Education

Low enrolment and high dropout track drought cycles as families migrate with herds; school-meals programmes and low-cost boarding ('lchekuti' model) are the main retention tools. PACIDA runs education access programmes across the county.
Conflict & peace

Resource-based and political flashpoints: Moyale corridor, Turbi–Forolle, and the Marsabit mountain belt (Borana–Gabra dynamics). Peace dividends directly determine access to dry-season grazing reserves. PACIDA facilitates inter-community resource-sharing dialogues and SMS Voices early warning.
marsabit.pacida: County HQ of PACIDA. Programmes: emergency drought response (water trucking, relief food, cash transfers), mass livestock deworming & treatment (480,000+ animals reached), WASH infrastructure, Ward Climate Change Planning Committees & County Climate Change Fund support, women's climate-resilience projects (Caritas Austria), education access, and peace & governance including the SMS Voices project with the County Government.

samburu.title: Samburu County
samburu.intro: A transition county between the central highlands and the northern deserts — 92% classified ASAL. From the Lorroki plateau and Kirisia forests around Maralal (2,000 m, agro-pastoral) the land falls north through Baragoi's Suguta corridor and east past the Mathews Range and Mt Ololokwe to the Ewaso Ng'iro lowlands at Archer's Post. The Samburu (Lokop) are cattle-culture pastoralists; drought forces herds into contested northern grazing where cattle rustling and armed conflict compound climate risk. Fewer than 15% of households have piped water.
subcounties: Kisima, Suguta Marmar, Loosuk, Poro, Morijo, Lodokejek
South Horr, Tuum, Marti, Nachola, Latakweny, Bendera
Archer's Post, Sereolipi, Lodungokwe, Ngilai, Lerata, Lpus
samburu.subnote: * 2019 census county totals are exact (310,327 people / 65,910 households); sub-county splits shown are indicative estimates pending ward-level tabulation.
sites: Nyiro valley, route to L. Turkana
sectors: Livestock economy

Cattle-dominant with rapid small-stock growth as a drought adaptation; camels are being adopted in the north. Key markets: Maralal, Baragoi, Archer's Post; trekking routes to Rumuruti/Nyahururu. Livestock body condition and milk yields collapse fastest in Samburu East lowlands.
Water & WASH

Only ~14% of households have piped water (2019 census). Sources: seasonal rivers (Ewaso Ng'iro), sand dams, boreholes, springs on the plateau. Dry-season water distances in Samburu East and North commonly exceed 10 km for households and 20 km for herds.
Nutrition & health

Acute malnutrition remains high in Samburu North (Tiaty-adjacent belt): NDMA lists Samburu among counties with significant numbers of children 6–59 months needing urgent treatment (Jan 2026). Milk deficit during dry seasons is the primary driver.
Education
Secondary attainment 6.4% — about a quarter of the national rate (2019 census). Morans' herding duties and early marriage suppress enrolment; conservancy bursaries and school feeding are key levers.
Conflict & peace

Cattle-rustling corridors: Baragoi–Suguta valley (Samburu–Turkana), and Samburu East–Isiolo boundary over Ewaso grazing. Disarmament cycles and peace committees shape whether drought reserves (Kirisia forest, Mathews Range) can be shared safely.
samburu.pacida: PACIDA implements resilience and emergency programming in Samburu: drought response (water, cash and fodder), WASH, livestock health campaigns, and cross-county peace dialogues linking Samburu, Marsabit and Isiolo grazing communities under the Humanitarian-Development-Peace nexus approach.

isiolo.title: Isiolo County
isiolo.gam: 12–18%; severe acute malnutrition cases documented in 2026 drought reporting
isiolo.intro: The gateway to northern Kenya and a melting pot of Borana, Turkana, Somali, Meru and Samburu communities. The county straddles the Ewaso Ng'iro river — the lifeline that carries highland water into the drylands and around which people, livestock and wildlife concentrate in every drought. Isiolo town is booming (A2 tarmac, abattoir, planned resort city under LAPSSET) while Merti and Garbatulla remain deep pastoral country. Isiolo was among the worst-hit counties in the 2023 floods and slid back into drought Alert through 2025–26 — the classic ASAL whiplash of failed rains and flash floods.
subcounties: Kambi Garba, Kiwanjani, Checheles, Burat, Ngare Mara, Gambella, Oldonyiro, Kipsing
Kinna, Rapsu, Kulamawe, Belgesh, Sericho, Boji, Duse
Korbesa, Bulesa, Biliqo, Malkadaka, Dadacha Basa, Mata Arba
sectors: Livestock economy

Borana cattle heartland with growing camel herds. Isiolo livestock market and the export abattoir anchor offtake; in drought, herds converge on the Ewaso riverine strip and Meru NP border, driving disease transmission and human-wildlife conflict.
Water & WASH

The Ewaso Ng'iro's flow is falling from upstream highland abstraction — the county's central climate-security issue. Flagship response: Merti–Korbesa water supply project (NDMA/EU/NWWDA/County). Elsewhere: boreholes, pans; Sericho and Cherab wards face the longest dry-season distances.
Nutrition & health

2026 drought reporting documented severe acute malnutrition cases in Isiolo; NDMA lists the county in Alert with worsening food access. GAM typically 12–18% in bad years, concentrated in Merti and Sericho.
Floods & multi-hazard

Isiolo is the textbook twin-disaster county: among the worst affected by the 2023 El Niño floods (Ewaso burst its banks, displacing riverine villages) followed directly by failed rains. Preparedness must cover both extremes.
Conflict & peace

Grazing pressure funnels Borana, Somali, Samburu and Turkana herds into the same riverine reserves; flashpoints on the Isiolo–Samburu (Oldonyiro) and Isiolo–Garissa (Modogashe–Sericho) axes. Land speculation along LAPSSET adds a new conflict layer.
isiolo.pacida: PACIDA scaled up in Isiolo after the 2023 floods put the organisation on the response frontline. Programmes: flood and drought emergency response, WASH, resilience building with Ward Climate Change Planning Committees, livestock health, and peace dialogues on shared Ewaso grazing.

borena.title: Borena Zone
borena.gam: Persistently elevated; SAM admissions surged in 2022–23 drought and remain above pre-drought baselines
borena.intro: The Ethiopian half of PACIDA's cross-border footprint and the cultural heartland of the Borana Oromo, whose Gadaa governance system (UNESCO-listed) and deep-well 'tula' system — the famous singing wells — have managed these rangelands for five centuries. The zone lost an estimated 60%+ of cattle in the catastrophic 2020–23 drought (five consecutive failed seasons), a livelihood shock from which herds have not recovered. Rainfall is bimodal: Ganna long rains (Mar–May) and Hagayya short rains (Oct–Nov). Cross-border movement with Marsabit County (Moyale, Dukana–Dillo, Forolle) is constant — grazing, trade, kinship and conflict all flow across the line, which is why single-country programming fails here.
subcounties: Dida Hara, Surupa, Dharito, Elwaye road
Sarite, El Gof, Konso border kebeles
borena.subnote: † Woreda figures are indicative projections from the 2007 CSA census pending a new national census; zone totals (~1.21 M people, ~232,000 households) are population-projection based. Boundary on the map is approximate.
sectors: Livestock economy

Cattle are wealth, identity and food security; the 2020–23 drought killed an estimated 3.3+ million livestock across Borena and neighbouring zones, collapsing herd capital. Restocking, fodder value-chains and shifting toward camels/small stock are the recovery frontier. Moyale is the region's cross-border trade artery.
Water & the tula system

The nine tula deep-well clusters (Dubluk, Mega, Web among them) are communally governed and drought-proof but labour-intensive; motorised boreholes and ponds (haro) supplement them. Water governance through Gadaa institutions is a resilience asset most interventions should build on, not replace.
Nutrition & health

SAM admissions surged through 2022–23 and stabilisation-centre caseloads remain above pre-drought baselines; measles and cholera outbreaks tracked displacement into IDP sites around Dubluk and Yabelo during the drought peak.
Rangelands & bush encroachment

Decades of fire suppression drove acacia/commiphora bush encroachment over prime grasslands — a slow-onset crisis reducing carrying capacity independent of rainfall. Participatory rangeland management and controlled clearing are priority interventions.
Conflict & cross-border dynamics

Borana–Gabra and Borana–Garre dynamics span the Kenya line; Moyale town has repeatedly split along it. Peace here is a precondition for drought-cycle mobility — closed borders during conflict episodes have trapped herds away from reserve grazing with fatal results.
borena.pacida: PACIDA's Ethiopian office anchors cross-border programming: drought emergency response, WASH around the tula clusters, livestock health, education support, and Borana-led peace and resource-sharing dialogues that keep the Marsabit–Borena grazing corridors open. Funded partners include Welthungerhilfe and BMZ programmes.

baringo.title: Baringo County
baringo.intro: Baringo straddles Kenya's Rift Valley floor and the Tugen Hills escarpment, running from Lake Bogoria's flamingo-lined shores and the hot springs at Loboi to the arid plains of Tiaty in the north-east. Around county HQ Kabarnet and the Eldama Ravine highlands, smallholder farmers grow maize, wheat and dairy on fertile volcanic soils; drop into the Kerio Valley or East Pokot and the economy turns pastoral, cattle- and goat-based, and chronically exposed to drought and cross-border banditry with neighbouring West Pokot. Geothermal exploration around Lake Bogoria and the Perkerra irrigation scheme near Marigat hint at untapped potential in a county that is, geographically, two very different Kenyas within one boundary.
subcounties: Chemolingot, Kolowa, Tangulbei, Nginyang, Silale, Churo
Marigat, Mochongoi, Ilchamus, Lake Baringo shore, Loboi
Eldama Ravine, Mumberes, Esageri, Timboroa border
baringo.subnote: County totals (666,763 people / 138,701 households) are the 2019 census figures; sub-county population and household splits are indicative estimates apportioned from constituency-level data pending full ward-level tabulation.
sites: Baringo South — Perkerra irrigation, Lake Baringo
Geothermal prospects, flamingo tourism, hot springs
livelihoods: Agro-pastoral & mixed farming (Central, North, Ravine, Mogotio)
sectors: Livestock & rangelands

Cattle and goats dominate lowland Baringo South and Tiaty, where East Pokot pastoralists depend on the Kerio Valley's sparse grazing and seasonal migration to the Tugen Hills escarpment during drought. Kabarnet and Eldama Ravine livestock markets link herders to Nakuru and Eldoret trade routes. Recurrent dry spells and shrinking communal grazing land, compounded by charcoal-driven deforestation, are steadily reducing carrying capacity across the county's pastoral wards.
Water, irrigation & the Rift lakes

The Perkerra irrigation scheme near Marigat supplies onions and horticulture from the Perkerra River, while Lake Baringo and Lake Bogoria anchor fishing, tourism and geothermal exploration interest. Elsewhere, boreholes, water pans and the seasonal Kerio River are the main sources; Tiaty's dispersed pastoral settlements face the county's longest dry-season trekking distances for both people and herds.
Nutrition, drought & security

East Pokot (Tiaty) periodically registers malnutrition and food-insecurity spikes comparable to classic ASAL counties further north, driven by drought and chronic insecurity. Cattle-rustling and banditry along the Kerio Valley and Baringo–Laikipia axis repeatedly disrupt markets, displace households and restrict humanitarian access, making conflict as significant a driver of vulnerability here as rainfall failure.
Highland agriculture & tourism potential

Kabarnet, Eldama Ravine and the Tugen Hills support maize, wheat, dairy and increasingly avocado farming on fertile volcanic soils, giving the county a genuine high-potential agricultural core alongside its dryland half. Lake Bogoria's flamingos, hot springs and geothermal prospects, plus growing honey and beekeeping enterprises, represent under-exploited diversification opportunities for a county straddling two very different economies.

embu.title: Embu County
embu.gam: 6–10% in Mbeere during drought years; rest of county not a nutrition hotspot
embu.intro: Embu county rises from the eastern slopes of Mt Kenya down through coffee-and-tea highlands around Embu town and Runyenjes to the semi-arid Mbeere plains along the Tana River. The upper county is classic high-potential central Kenya farmland — coffee, tea, macadamia, miraa and dairy support relatively low poverty and dense, well-serviced settlement. Mbeere North and South, by contrast, are genuinely ASAL: thorn-scrub rangeland where sorghum, millet and livestock are the norm and drought bites hard in poor rainfall years, moderated somewhat by the Tana's Kiambere and Masinga hydro-dams that sit within county boundaries. Embu is, in miniature, the same wet-highland-to-dry-lowland gradient found in Meru and Kitui — one county, two climates.
subcounties: Urban/peri-urban & coffee-tea highland farming — county HQ
embu.subnote: Embu has 4 official sub-counties/constituencies, all listed above. County totals (608,599 people / 174,750 households) reflect the 2019 census; sub-county splits are indicative estimates apportioned from constituency-level data pending full ward-level tabulation.
sectors: Highland cash crops

Coffee, tea, macadamia and miraa farming around Embu town, Runyenjes and the Mt Kenya foothills anchor a relatively prosperous agricultural economy, supported by cooperative societies and factory processing. These export cash crops, alongside dairy and horticulture, keep poverty in Manyatta and Runyenjes well below the national average.
Mbeere drylands

Mbeere North and South are Embu's genuine ASAL zone: thorn-scrub rangeland where sorghum, millet, green grams and livestock rearing are the norm, and food insecurity rises sharply in poor rainfall years. Distances to water and markets are far longer here than in the wetter highland sub-counties, despite sharing a single county government.
Water & hydropower

The Tana River's Kiambere and neighbouring Masinga dams sit within or adjoining Embu, feeding national hydropower generation, while irrigation potential along the river remains only partly developed. Mbeere's water access is the county's central climate-adaptation challenge, contrasted with relatively reliable highland rainfall further north; expanding small-scale irrigation off the Tana and its tributaries is a recurring county development priority.
A county of two climates

Embu compresses, within one boundary, the same wet-highland-to-dry-lowland gradient found across central and eastern Kenya's mixed ASAL counties: Manyatta and Runyenjes resemble high-potential Kirinyaga or Murang'a, while Mbeere resembles neighbouring Kitui or Tharaka-Nithi's drier belts. Differentiated, sub-county-specific programming is essential rather than optional here.

garissa.title: Garissa County
garissa.gam: 15–22% (Fafi, Ijara & Dadaab highest, recent SMART surveys)
garissa.intro: Garissa is the commercial and administrative heart of North Eastern Kenya, a Somali-majority county straddling the Tana River where it cuts through semi-desert scrub on its way to the Indian Ocean. Camel and cattle pastoralism underpins most household income, concentrated along the river's riverine strip in Balambala and Fafi where flood-recession farming is possible; away from the river, life is classic dryland pastoralism vulnerable to both drought and, increasingly, Tana flooding. The county has hosted the Dadaab refugee camp complex — among the largest in the world — for over three decades, a demographic and economic fact that shapes local markets, aid flows and service delivery as much as any climate indicator.
subcounties: Urban/peri-urban riverine trade (Tana River) — county HQ
Dadaab town, Dagahaley, Hagadera, Ifo camps
garissa.subnote: County totals (841,353 people / 116,204 households) reflect the 2019 census. Sub-county splits are indicative estimates apportioned from constituency-level data; Dadaab's figures reflect host-community population and exclude the separately enumerated refugee-camp population.
sites: Refugee camp complex — Dagahaley, Hagadera, Ifo
sectors: Livestock economy

Camel and cattle pastoralism underpins most rural household income; Garissa's livestock market is among the largest trading points in North Eastern Kenya, linking herders to Nairobi and export markets via the A3 corridor. Drought-driven herd losses and disease outbreaks remain the county's dominant economic shock, with recovery periods stretching over several dry seasons before herd sizes rebuild.
Tana River & floods

Garissa Township, Balambala and Fafi sit on the Tana floodplain, where flood-recession farming supports maize, cowpeas and vegetables in good years but flash flooding — as seen in the 2023 El Niño season — regularly displaces riverside communities directly after or even during drought, a dual-hazard pattern that complicates emergency response planning.
Dadaab & refugee-hosting dynamics

The Dadaab camp complex — Dagahaley, Hagadera and Ifo — has hosted, at various points, several hundred thousand refugees for over three decades, shaping local markets, service delivery and land use far beyond the camps themselves. Host-community and refugee vulnerability are closely intertwined, and UNHCR/WFP programming is central to the county's humanitarian architecture.
Nutrition & water

GAM rates in Fafi, Ijara and around Dadaab regularly approach or exceed WHO emergency thresholds during poor rainy seasons, driven by milk deficits as herds move away from homesteads. Borehole and water-trucking dependency is high across the county's non-riverine wards, and water-point breakdown is a recurring driver of localised crisis.

kajiado.title: Kajiado County
kajiado.intro: Kajiado is Kenya's fastest-urbanising ASAL county, its northern wards — Ongata Rongai, Kiserian, Kitengela, Isinya — now dense Nairobi commuter suburbs sitting inside what remains, on paper, classic Maasai rangeland. Drive an hour south, however, and the county reverts to the pastoralism, dispersed manyattas and open grassland of Kajiado Central, West and South, home to Amboseli National Park's iconic Mt Kilimanjaro backdrop and the Magadi soda-ash works on the shores of Lake Magadi. Land subdivision, wildlife conservancies and urban sprawl are eroding traditional grazing commons faster than in almost any other Maasai county, even as tourism and Nairobi-adjacent real estate give Kajiado significantly lower poverty than its ASAL neighbours further north.
subcounties: Ongata Rongai, Ngong, Kiserian, Ngong Hills
Loitokitok, Kimana, Rombo, Amboseli NP fringe
kajiado.subnote: County totals (1,117,840 people / 313,433 households) reflect the 2019 census; sub-county splits are indicative estimates apportioned from constituency-level data pending full ward-level tabulation.
sectors: Livestock & rangelands

Maasai cattle and shoat pastoralism remains the backbone of Kajiado Central, West and South's rural economy, though land subdivision, fencing and the loss of communal grazing corridors are steadily reducing herd mobility and drought resilience compared to a generation ago. Drought years push herders into conservancies and neighbouring counties in search of pasture.
Nairobi-adjacent urbanisation

Ongata Rongai, Kiserian, Kitengela and Isinya have become some of Kenya's fastest-growing commuter towns, absorbing Nairobi's overflow population and transforming Kajiado North and East from pastoral rangeland into dense residential and light-industrial suburbs within little more than two decades — a land-use shift with few parallels elsewhere in ASAL Kenya.
Tourism & conservation

Amboseli National Park, its Mt Kilimanjaro backdrop and a dense network of community wildlife conservancies in Kajiado South generate significant tourism revenue and conservancy-lease income for Maasai landowners, though human-wildlife conflict and competition between grazing and wildlife land use remain persistent friction points, especially during drought, when both livestock and wildlife concentrate around the same shrinking water points.
Water & industry

Kajiado West and South face recurring dry-season water stress despite the county's proximity to Nairobi's own water infrastructure; the Magadi soda-ash works on Lake Magadi's shores is a major industrial employer and revenue source that itself depends on a fragile, highly saline lake ecosystem sensitive to rainfall variability.

kilifi.title: Kilifi County
kilifi.gam: 9–15% in drought years (Ganze and Magarini highest)
kilifi.intro: Kilifi is Kenya's coast-versus-hinterland ASAL in miniature. Along the Indian Ocean, Malindi's historic Swahili-Portuguese town, Watamu's marine park and the Kilifi Creek beach belt anchor a globally known tourism economy just a few kilometres from the semi-arid Mijikenda hinterland of Ganze and Magarini, where erratic rains regularly push maize and livestock-dependent households into food insecurity. Cashew, coconut and copra have long been the coastal-belt mainstays, though ageing trees and disease have eroded returns. The Arabuko-Sokoke Forest, the largest surviving fragment of East Africa's coastal forest, sits between the two worlds as a globally significant biodiversity reserve. NDMA classifies Kilifi's interior wards among the county's most food-insecure in most years.
kilifi.subnote: Sub-county totals are 2019 census constituency-level figures for Kilifi's 7 constituencies; households derived using the county average household size (indicative pending full ward tabulation).
sectors: Coast tourism & fisheries

Malindi, Watamu and the Kilifi Creek beach belt anchor a globally known tourism economy (marine parks, historic Swahili/Portuguese heritage at Gede and Malindi), alongside artisanal fishing along the reef and creek systems — a stark contrast to the arid hinterland a few kilometres inland.
Rain-fed agriculture & tree crops

Cashew nut, coconut/copra and maize are the historic mainstays of the coastal-belt Mijikenda economy, but ageing trees, crop disease and erratic short rains have pushed many households toward casual coastal labour and small trade.
Hinterland food security

Ganze, Magarini and parts of Kaloleni sit in the semi-arid hinterland where maize and livestock depend on increasingly unreliable rains; NDMA classifies these wards among Kilifi's most food-insecure areas most years, with GAM rising sharply after poor seasons.
Water, land & forest

The Arabuko-Sokoke Forest is a globally significant biodiversity site under pressure from charcoal and farmland expansion; countywide, groundwater salinity and long dry-season water-trekking distances remain persistent hinterland challenges.

kitui.title: Kitui County
kitui.phase: NDMA Alarm (localized — Mwingi North & Kitui South)
kitui.gam: 10–16% in drought years (Mwingi North and Kitui South highest)
kitui.intro: Kitui is classic semi-arid Ukambani, a vast Kamba county of drought-tolerant sorghum, millet, pigeon peas and Kenya's leading green-gram (ndengu) crop, grown across two unreliable rain seasons that fail almost as often as they deliver. Goats, cattle and a growing camel presence underpin household resilience. Kitui pioneered Kenya's community sand-dam movement, with thousands of dams built across seasonal riverbeds — a globally cited model for locally led water harvesting. Beekeeping and honey production add a modest but valued cash income, and the long-delayed Mui Basin coal deposits represent a potentially transformative but still-undeveloped resource. NDMA regularly places Kitui's northern and southern sub-counties in Alert or worse during poor rainfall years.
kitui.subnote: Sub-county figures are indicative 2019 census constituency-level estimates for Kitui's 8 constituencies, apportioning the county total pending full ward-level tabulation.
sectors: Drought-tolerant agriculture

Kitui leads Kenya in green gram (ndengu) production and is a major producer of sorghum, millet, pigeon peas and cowpeas — crops selected over generations for the county's erratic, often-failing rains. Two rain seasons mean two chances for crop failure most years.
Water harvesting & sand dams

Kitui pioneered Kenya's sand-dam movement, with Utooni Development Organisation and partners building thousands of dams across the county's seasonal riverbeds — a globally cited model for community-led water harvesting that has measurably reduced dry-season fetching distances.
Livestock & food security

Goats, some cattle and a growing camel presence underpin household resilience alongside crops; NDMA regularly classifies Kitui sub-counties, especially Mwingi North and Kitui South, in Alert or worse during poor rainfall years.
Minerals & emerging economy

The Mui Basin coal deposits represent a long-delayed but potentially transformative resource; beekeeping and honey production (Kitui honey has a strong regional brand) and a growing horticulture trade toward Nairobi are smaller diversification pathways away from rain-fed dependence.

kwale.title: Kwale County
kwale.intro: Kwale is Kenya's southernmost coastal county, straddling a lush, tourism-rich coastline and an arid Digo-Duruma interior. Diani Beach anchors one of East Africa's premier tourism destinations, and Shimba Hills National Reserve is the only place in Kenya home to the sable antelope. Base Titanium's Kwale Mineral Sands operation, one of the country's largest single export earners, sits inland of the beach strip. Coconut, cashew and maize sustain the coastal-belt economy, while Kinango and Lunga Lunga's semi-arid interior depends on erratic rains for maize and livestock, regularly drawing NDMA food-security concern. Lunga Lunga is also Kenya's main southern land border crossing with Tanzania, generating substantial informal cross-border trade.
kwale.subnote: Sub-county totals correspond to 2019 census constituency-level figures for Kwale's 4 constituencies; households derived using the county average household size.
sectors: Coastal tourism

The Diani Beach corridor is one of East Africa's premier tourism destinations (dive tourism, resort hotels, Shimba Hills National Reserve) driving hospitality employment along the coastal strip in Msambweni and Matuga, even as the arid interior remains food-insecure.
Mining

Base Titanium's Kwale Mineral Sands operation, spanning Kinango and Msambweni, is one of Kenya's largest single export earners and a major local employer and county revenue source, alongside ongoing land-compensation and resettlement issues for displaced communities.
Rain-fed & hinterland agriculture

Coconut, cashew and maize sustain the Digo-Duruma coastal-belt economy, while Kinango and Lungalunga's semi-arid interior depends on erratic rains for maize and livestock; NDMA regularly flags Kinango among Kwale's most food-insecure areas during poor rainfall seasons.
Cross-border trade & water

Lunga Lunga is Kenya's main southern land-border crossing with Tanzania, generating significant informal cross-border trade; countywide, groundwater salinity intrusion along the coast and long dry-season trekking distances in Kinango's interior are persistent water-security challenges.

laikipia.title: Laikipia County
laikipia.phase: NDMA Normal (localized concern in Laikipia North)
laikipia.gam: 6–11% in Laikipia North (Mukogodo/Il Ngwesi); not a hotspot elsewhere in the county
laikipia.intro: Laikipia sprawls across the high plateau between Mt Kenya and the Rift Valley escarpment, a mosaic of large-scale wheat and barley farms, cattle ranches and some of Africa's most celebrated wildlife conservancies — Ol Pejeta (a rhino sanctuary) and Lewa (a UNESCO World Heritage Site) both sit within its borders. Nanyuki, the county's commercial hub at Mt Kenya's northern foot, has grown fast on tourism, flower export and a British Army training presence. The south and centre are high-potential agricultural land, but the northern rangelands around Dol Dol, Mukogodo and Il Ngwesi are true ASAL, home to Maasai and Samburu pastoralists whose herds compete with wildlife for dry-season grazing and water drawn from the Ewaso Ng'iro headwaters that downstream Isiolo and Samburu depend on.
subcounties: Nanyuki, Timau, Naromoru, Ol Pejeta, Sweetwaters
Rumuruti, Nyahururu, Ol Moran, Marmanet, Salama
Dol Dol, Il Ngwesi, Mukogodo, Naibor, Sosian
laikipia.subnote: 2019 census county totals are exact (518,560 people / 147,347 households); sub-county splits shown are indicative estimates pending ward-level tabulation.
sites: County HQ area — commercial & tourism hub at Mt Kenya's northern foot
Laikipia West — county administrative HQ town
sectors: Agriculture & large-scale ranching

Commercial wheat, barley and seed-potato farms and large cattle ranches (many overlapping wildlife conservancies) dominate the county's centre and west. Laikipia is one of Kenya's most productive dryland-agriculture zones, but rainfall is erratic and land-use planning between ranching, farming and conservancy interests is a constant negotiation, especially during dry years when grazing pressure spikes.
Wildlife conservation & tourism

Ol Pejeta Conservancy (East Africa's largest black rhino sanctuary and home to the world's last northern white rhinos) and the UNESCO-listed Lewa Wildlife Conservancy anchor a globally significant conservation economy. Community and private conservancies cover roughly a third of the county, generating tourism revenue and conservation jobs, though human-wildlife conflict rises sharply whenever drought pushes wildlife and livestock onto the same shrinking pastures.
Water & the Ewaso Ng'iro headwaters

Laikipia sits astride the headwaters of the Ewaso Ng'iro river system that Isiolo, Samburu and Garissa depend on downstream. Upstream irrigation and commercial abstraction by farms and flower growers have repeatedly reduced dry-season flow, a persistent source of tension with downstream pastoralist counties and the subject of ongoing water-allocation negotiations facilitated by the Ewaso Ng'iro Water Resource Users Association.
Northern pastoral drylands & conflict

Laikipia North's Mukogodo forest and community conservancies (Il Ngwesi, Naibunga) are Maasai and Samburu pastoral country, the county's only NDMA-monitored ASAL belt. Drought years push herds onto neighbouring ranches and conservancies, occasionally triggering land invasions and cattle-rustling episodes that have periodically made national headlines; peace committees and grazing agreements between ranch owners and pastoralist communities are the main mitigation tool.

lamu.title: Lamu County
lamu.gam: 8–14% (Lamu East highest, fishing/pastoral pockets & insecurity-affected areas)
lamu.intro: Kenya's northernmost coastal county and the cultural heart of the Swahili civilisation: Lamu Old Town, continuously inhabited for over 700 years, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site of coral-stone architecture and donkey-cart streets. Beyond the tourist draw of Lamu Island and Shela beach, the mainland is a mix of mangrove-fringed fishing creeks, the Mpeketoni settlement scheme's maize and coconut farms, and the remote Boni forest bordering Somalia — an area affected by recurrent Al-Shabaab activity that has repeatedly disrupted schooling, trade and humanitarian access in Lamu East. The county is also ground zero for the multi-billion-shilling LAPSSET Lamu Port project, whose planned 32 berths are reshaping the local economy even as fishing and small-scale farming remain the backbone of most households.
subcounties: Lamu town, Mokowe, Mpeketoni, Hindi, Witu, Shela
Faza, Kiunga, Kizingitini, Pate, Siyu, Ndau
lamu.subnote: 2019 census county totals are exact (143,920 people / 39,554 households); sub-county splits shown are indicative estimates pending ward-level tabulation.
sites: County HQ — UNESCO World Heritage Old Town
Mainland gateway to Lamu Island, near LAPSSET port
sectors: Fisheries & marine economy

Fishing sustains most coastal households — Lamu's mangrove creeks, seagrass beds and offshore waters support artisanal fishers using traditional dhows and traps around Lamu, Kiunga and Faza. Overfishing, mangrove degradation and competition from the new Lamu Port's dredging and shipping traffic are emerging pressures on a fishery that has otherwise changed little in generations.
Tourism & heritage

Lamu Old Town, continuously inhabited for over 700 years, is Kenya's oldest and best-preserved Swahili settlement and a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Dhow-building, donkey transport and coral-stone architecture draw a steady, if security-sensitive, tourist trade centred on Lamu Island and Shela beach — a vital income source alongside fishing for much of Lamu West.
Agriculture & the Mpeketoni scheme

The Mpeketoni settlement scheme on the mainland, established in the 1970s, is Lamu's main farming zone — maize, coconut, cashew, mango and cattle. Rainfall is more reliable than in the deep interior ASAL counties but still erratic, and the scheme has repeatedly been a target of insecurity, disrupting harvests and displacing farming households in bad years.
Security & the LAPSSET port frontier

Lamu East (Boni forest, Hindi, Mpeketoni fringe) has suffered recurrent Al-Shabaab attacks and IED incidents since 2011, forcing school closures, curfews and population displacement. At the same time, the county hosts the multi-berth LAPSSET Lamu Port — a multi-billion-shilling national infrastructure project reshaping land values and employment even as security operations continue in the same sub-county.

makueni.title: Makueni County
makueni.intro: One of the three Ukambani counties and a national pioneer in community-led drought resilience: Makueni has built more sand dams — over 1,000 — than any other county in Africa, harvesting seasonal river flow to secure water and recharge groundwater through the dry months. Maize and legume farming is rain-fed and precarious across most of the county, but Kibwezi's irrigation schemes and the county-backed Kalamba fruit-processing plant have helped make mango and orange growing a genuine cash crop. Sand harvesting along the Kaiti and other seasonal rivers is a major, if environmentally contentious, livelihood. Wote, the county HQ, sits on the main Nairobi–Mombasa corridor, and Kibwezi's Tsavo West and Chyulu Hills frontier brings a modest tourism economy alongside the pastoral fringe.
makueni.subnote: 2019 census county totals are exact (987,653 people / 251,391 households); sub-county splits shown are indicative estimates pending ward-level tabulation.
sites: Kibwezi East, near Tsavo West/Chyulu Hills
sectors: Water harvesting & sand dams

Makueni has built more sand dams than any other county in Kenya — well over 1,000 — trapping seasonal river flow behind small concrete walls to recharge groundwater and secure dry-season water for households, livestock and small-scale irrigation. The model, pioneered with NGOs like the Africa Sand Dam Foundation, is now studied nationally and regionally as a low-cost drought-resilience technology.
Rain-fed agriculture & drought risk

Maize, beans, pigeon peas, sorghum and millet are grown across most of the county on rain-fed plots highly exposed to the two-season rainfall pattern's frequent failures. Fruit farming — mangoes and oranges especially — has expanded fast, supported by the county-backed Kalamba fruit-processing plant, giving households a more drought-tolerant cash crop alongside traditional staples.
Livestock & sand harvesting

Goats and some cattle are kept across the drier eastern wards (Kibwezi, Kathonzweni), providing a buffer when crops fail. Commercial sand harvesting along the Kaiti and other seasonal riverbeds is a major, if environmentally contentious, source of casual income and county revenue, with over-extraction blamed for river-bed degradation and water-table decline in places.
Tourism & the Tsavo/Chyulu frontier

Kibwezi's proximity to Tsavo West National Park and the Chyulu Hills brings a modest but growing tourism and conservancy economy, alongside the Nairobi–Mombasa highway trade that flows through Mtito Andei and Makindu. Wildlife corridors and human-wildlife conflict management are an increasing county planning concern as settlement expands toward the park boundary.

mandera.title: Mandera County
mandera.gam: 20–28% (Mandera East & Banissa historically highest, cross-border insecurity compounds access)
mandera.intro: Kenya's north-eastern frontier county, wedged into the tripoint where Kenya, Somalia and Ethiopia meet, and crossed by the Daua River that forms its northern boundary. Mandera has Kenya's largest average household size and among its highest poverty rates, reflecting a purely pastoral Somali economy built on camel, cattle, goat and sheep herds that move constantly across the porous borders in search of pasture and markets in Somalia and Ethiopia. Cross-border trade and large diaspora remittances supplement livestock income county-wide. The county has also borne the brunt of Al-Shabaab cross-border attacks and IED incidents along the Mandera–Ramu axis, which periodically disrupt trade, schooling and humanitarian access. Water is scarce and trekking distances for both people and herds are among the longest in the country.
mandera.subnote: 2019 census county totals are exact (867,457 people / 111,809 households); sub-county splits shown are indicative estimates pending ward-level tabulation.
livelihoods: Agro-pastoral (Daua river irrigation — El Wak, Rhamu)
sectors: Livestock economy & cross-border trade

Camel, cattle, goat and sheep herding underpins roughly four in five households, with animals and traders moving continuously across the porous Somalia and Ethiopia borders to markets, pasture and water. Mandera's livestock trade is deeply integrated with southern Somalia's and Ethiopia's economies, and remittances from a large diaspora supplement herd income county-wide.
Water & WASH

The seasonal Daua River, boreholes and shallow wells are the main water sources; in drought years households and herds in Lafey, Banissa and Mandera South routinely trek over 15–20 km. Water trucking and borehole rehabilitation are recurring NDMA and county emergency responses, and cross-border water-sharing arrangements with Somali and Ethiopian communities are an ongoing diplomatic necessity.
Nutrition & health

Mandera consistently records some of Kenya's highest Global Acute Malnutrition rates, with SMART surveys repeatedly breaching the WHO emergency threshold in Mandera East and Banissa during drought. Insecurity restricts humanitarian and health-worker access to parts of the county, compounding an already thin rural health infrastructure and driving reliance on outreach and mobile clinics.
Security & cross-border conflict

Recurrent Al-Shabaab attacks and IED incidents along the Mandera–Ramu and border axis, alongside periodic inter-clan disputes over grazing and water, make Mandera one of Kenya's most security-sensitive counties. Conflict episodes routinely close roads, disrupt trade convoys and displace communities, compounding drought impacts and constraining both humanitarian response and normal economic activity.

meru.title: Meru County
meru.phase: NDMA Alert (localized — northern Igembe North/Tigania East belt only)
meru.gam: 5–9% county-wide; up to 14% in Igembe North/Tigania East during drought years (rest of county not a nutrition hotspot)
meru.intro: Meru wraps around the northern and eastern flanks of Mt Kenya, and for most of its length is high-potential agricultural country — tea, coffee, dairy and, above all, miraa (khat): Maua, in Igembe, hosts East Africa's largest miraa market, feeding an export trade to Somalia worth billions of shillings annually. Meru town, the county HQ, anchors a dense highland economy of tea factories, banks and Mt Kenya-facing farms. Only the far northern fringe — Igembe North and parts of Tigania East, bordering Isiolo and Meru National Park — is true ASAL: semi-arid livestock country where drought occasionally pushes the area into NDMA Alert, even as the rest of the county remains firmly in Kenya's agricultural heartland.
meru.subnote: 2019 census county totals are exact (1,545,714 people / 384,180 households); sub-county splits shown are indicative estimates pending ward-level tabulation.
sites: Igembe Central — East Africa's largest miraa market
Igembe North — ASAL fringe near Isiolo
Tigania East — semi-arid, Meru NP border
livelihoods: Pastoral & agro-pastoral drylands (Igembe North/Tigania East fringe)
sectors: Miraa (khat) economy

Maua, in Igembe Central, hosts East Africa's largest miraa (khat) market, the centre of a cash-crop trade worth billions of shillings annually and a major source of formal and informal employment across Igembe and Tigania. Export markets in Somalia are the trade's lifeline, and the crop's resilience to erratic rainfall makes it a preferred hedge against crop failure.
Tea, coffee & dairy farming

The Imenti and Buuri highlands around Mt Kenya's northern slopes are prime tea and coffee country, feeding numerous local factories, alongside intensive smallholder dairy farming that supplies Meru town's processors and the national milk market. This highland belt is what makes Meru, overall, one of Kenya's more food-secure and higher-income agricultural counties.
Water towers & natural resources

Mt Kenya and Imenti forests feed the rivers that irrigate Meru's highland farms and, further downstream, sustain Isiolo and Tana basin communities. Illegal logging, forest excisions and charcoal burning on the forest fringe are longstanding conservation concerns that the county and Kenya Forest Service actively police, given the basin-wide dependence on these headwaters.
Northern drylands & drought risk

Igembe North (Laare) and parts of Tigania East, bordering Isiolo and Meru National Park, are semi-arid livestock country and Meru's only NDMA-monitored ASAL fringe. Drought here can push the sub-counties into Alert status even as the rest of Meru remains agriculturally secure, making targeted rather than county-wide drought response the appropriate policy tool.

narok.title: Narok County
narok.phase: NDMA Alert (localized — Narok South & Trans Mara pastoral wards)
narok.gam: 9–15% in Narok South/Trans Mara pastoral wards during drought years; lower in the wheat-farming north
narok.intro: Narok stretches from the wheat-covered Mau plains in the north to the acacia savannah of the Maasai Mara in the south, Kenya's premier wildlife-tourism county and a Maasai pastoral heartland. Cattle, sheep and goats remain central to Maasai livelihoods and culture, while community conservancies bordering the Maasai Mara National Reserve generate some of the country's largest wildlife-tourism revenues. Mechanised wheat and barley farming on the Mau/Narok plains adds a substantial commercial-agriculture dimension rare among ASAL counties. The Mau Forest Complex, source of the Mara River, is the county's critical — and increasingly threatened — water tower. Narok's southern and eastern pastoral rangelands carry NDMA/ASAL classification, distinguishing them from the wetter, higher-potential north.
subcounties: Kilgoris town, Angata Barrikoi, Lolgorian road
narok.subnote: Sub-county splits are indicative apportionments of the 2019 county totals (1,157,873 people / 251,834 households) pending full ward-level tabulation.
sites: Maasai Mara Game Reserve — wildlife tourism gateway
Rift floor — wheat/pastoral boundary with Nakuru
sectors: Livestock & pastoral economy

Cattle remain central to Maasai identity and wealth across Narok South, West and Trans Mara; small-stock (sheep/goats) provide a faster-liquidating buffer in drought years. Herds move seasonally between the Loita hills, Mau forest fringe and Mara plains as pasture and water allow.
Wildlife tourism & conservancies

The Maasai Mara National Reserve and adjoining community conservancies (Mara Naboisho, Olare Motorogi, Ol Kinyei) are one of Kenya's top foreign-exchange earners and a major source of land-lease income and employment for Maasai landowners, though benefit-sharing and human-wildlife conflict remain live issues.
Mechanised agriculture

The Mau/Narok plains around Narok North and Narok East host some of Kenya's largest mechanised wheat and barley farms, making the county a significant national grain producer alongside its pastoral economy.
Water, forest & environment

The Mau Forest Complex, a critical water tower feeding the Mara River and Lake Victoria basin, has suffered significant deforestation from settlement and logging; resulting siltation and reduced dry-season flows threaten both the Mara ecosystem's tourism value and downstream pastoral water access.

nyeri.title: Nyeri County
nyeri.phase: NDMA Normal (Kieni sub-county only classified ASAL)
nyeri.gam: Low county-wide; localized elevated risk in Kieni's semi-arid wards (Mweiga, Naromoru, Kabaru) during dry seasons
nyeri.intro: Nyeri is the classic Mt Kenya highlands county, one of the country's most productive coffee and tea heartlands, straddling the fertile slopes between Mt Kenya and the Aberdare Range. Karatina, Othaya and Mukurweini anchor a smallholder cash-crop and dairy economy long organised through cooperative societies. The exception is Kieni sub-county on the drier, rain-shadow eastern flank facing Laikipia — Kenya's only NDMA/ASAL-classified pocket in Nyeri, given over to wheat, extensive livestock and wildlife-conservancy land uses. Nyeri is also historically significant, tied to Mau Mau history and Dedan Kimathi's capture, and to the Kenyatta family home in Othaya.
nyeri.subnote: Sub-county splits are indicative apportionments of the 2019 county totals (759,164 people / 237,239 households) pending full ward-level tabulation.
sites: Kieni — drier ranching/wheat zone, KWS HQ
sectors: Coffee & tea economy

Nyeri is one of Kenya's historic coffee heartlands — Othaya, Mathira and Mukurweini are anchored by long-established cooperative societies (including some of the country's highest-earning factories) alongside smallholder tea on the wetter western wards.
Dairy farming
High-grade Friesian and Ayrshire herds under zero-grazing are near-universal supplementary income; well-established milk cooperatives give the county one of Kenya's more developed dairy value chains.
Kieni's semi-arid duality

Kieni sub-county, on the drier, rain-shadow eastern flank facing Laikipia, is Nyeri's only NDMA/ASAL-classified area — given over to wheat, extensive livestock ranching and irrigated horticulture, with periodic water stress and human-wildlife conflict from the Mt Kenya/Aberdare-Solio wildlife corridor distinguishing it sharply from the wetter coffee highlands to the west.
Tourism & conservation

Nyeri anchors the southern gateway to Mt Kenya National Park (Naro Moru route) and borders the Aberdare National Park and Solio/Sweetwaters conservancies in Kieni, giving the county a meaningful wildlife-tourism sector alongside its agricultural economy.

taita-taveta.title: Taita Taveta County
taita-taveta.gam: 6–11% (Voi and Sagalla lowlands highest in dry years)
taita-taveta.intro: Taita Taveta straddles the coastal hinterland between Mombasa and the Rift Valley, dominated by the misty Taita Hills and the vast plains of Tsavo East and Tsavo West national parks, which together cover over half the county's land. Voi, on the Nairobi–Mombasa highway and railway, is the commercial hub, while Wundanyi sits cooler in the hills. Livelihoods split sharply: intensive horticulture and dairy in the Taita Hills' fertile micro-climates versus semi-arid ranching, sisal estates and wildlife-based tourism on the surrounding lowlands. Human-wildlife conflict along the Tsavo corridors is a defining management challenge, alongside chronic water scarcity outside the hills, and small-scale gemstone mining (tsavorite, tourmaline) is a growing informal income source.
subcounties: Mwatate town, Bura, Rong'e, Chala road
Taveta town, Chala, Njoro, Lake Chala
taita-taveta.subnote: Sub-county population splits are indicative estimates apportioned from the 2019 county totals (340,671 people / 100,743 households); ward-level KNBS tabulation is not fully public.
sites: County HQ — rail town, Tsavo gateway
Taita Hills forest fringe, water tower
sectors: Wildlife economy & human-wildlife conflict

Tsavo East and West cover more than 60% of the county's land, anchoring a major tourism economy but also producing chronic crop-raiding and livestock predation along the Mwatate–Rukanga and Sagalla corridors. KWS compensation schemes and community conservancies are the main mitigation tools, though payouts routinely lag losses.
Highland agriculture

The Taita Hills' fertile, high-rainfall micro-climate supports intensive horticulture (tomatoes, bananas, a fast-growing avocado export trade) and dairy, but extreme land fragmentation and steep-slope farming drive soil erosion. Yields here are among the highest per hectare in the wider coastal region.
Water & irrigation

Lowland Voi and Mwatate depend on the seasonal Voi and Mwatate rivers, boreholes and water pans for people and livestock; Taveta draws on the more reliable Lumi River and Lake Chala springs, supporting irrigated maize and rice. WASH coverage drops sharply outside the hills.
Livelihoods & poverty

Declining sisal estates, once the county's largest formal employer, have left youth unemployment concentrated in Voi and Taveta towns. Small-scale gemstone mining (tsavorite, tourmaline, ruby) around Mwatate and Voi supplements pastoral and farming incomes but remains largely informal and unregulated.

tana-river.title: Tana River County
tana-river.gam: 12–19% (Galole and Bura riverine highest, post-flood spikes)
tana-river.intro: Tana River County follows Kenya's longest river from the Tana Delta wetlands on the Indian Ocean coast upstream through Hola and Bura toward the Tsavo hinterland — one of Kenya's most flood- and drought-prone counties, alternating between the two extremes almost every year. The Pokomo farm the riverine floodplain while the Orma and Wardei graze cattle and camels on the surrounding semi-arid bush; competition between the two livelihoods over the same narrow green corridor produced some of Kenya's deadliest resource conflicts, notably the 2012–13 Tana Delta clashes. The Delta's mangroves, ranches and the long-underutilised Bura and Hola irrigation schemes make it a county of major undeveloped agricultural potential.
subcounties: Garsen town, Kipini, Ozi, Tana Delta
tana-river.subnote: Sub-county splits are indicative estimates apportioned from the 2019 county totals (315,943 people / 59,612 households); ward-level tabulation is not fully public.
sectors: Flood & drought whiplash

Tana River is Kenya's classic twin-hazard county: El Niño-driven floods burst the river's banks and displace riverine villages, often followed directly by drought when the same rains fail elsewhere. NDMA and county response plans must budget for both extremes within a single season.
Livestock & farmer-herder conflict

Historic Orma–Pokomo clashes over grazing versus farmland in the Tana Delta, including the deadly 2012–13 violence, remain a live fault line. Peace committees, delta land-use planning and formalised grazing corridors are central to any resilience programming here.
Irrigation potential

The stalled and underutilised Bura and Hola irrigation schemes represent one of Kenya's largest unrealised food-security assets. Rehabilitation, TARDA's mandate over the schemes, and Delta rice and cotton proposals recur in every county development plan but await sustained investment.
Water & health

Most households rely directly on the Tana River, shallow wells and seasonal pans. Waterborne disease and malaria track the flood cycle closely, while GAM rises sharply in Bura and Galole during drought years and after floods disrupt food access.

tharaka-nithi.title: Tharaka-Nithi County
tharaka-nithi.gam: 7–12% (Tharaka North & South lowlands; Chuka/Maara highlands not a hotspot)
tharaka-nithi.intro: Tharaka-Nithi is a county of two climates on the eastern slopes of Mt Kenya. Chuka, Maara and Igambang'ombe sit in fertile, well-watered mid-highlands where tea, coffee, miraa and bananas thrive — among the most productive smallholder land in eastern Kenya. Cross the Thanantu escarpment north-east, however, and the land drops onto the hot, dry Tharaka plains, semi-arid bushland classified ASAL where sorghum, millet, goats and honey are the mainstay and drought is a recurring shock. The Thuci, Mutonga and Thingithu rivers rise in these highlands, feeding the Kiambere hydropower dam downstream. Miraa is a major cash earner region-wide, tying local incomes to volatile export demand.
tharaka-nithi.subnote: Sub-county splits are indicative estimates apportioned from the 2019 county totals (393,177 people / 106,264 households); only Tharaka North and Tharaka South are ASAL-classified.
sectors: Highland–lowland duality

Chuka and Maara's reliable rainfall (1,200mm+) supports intensive tea and coffee smallholdings, while Tharaka North and South, under 700mm of erratic rain, are classified ASAL with sorghum, millet, goats and honey the norm. Development planning here has to run two completely different playbooks.
Miraa economy

Miraa (khat) is a major cash crop bridging both zones, feeding the Maua and onward Nairobi/export markets. Household incomes tied to miraa are volatile, swinging with export-market access (notably to Somalia) and periodic bans in destination countries.
Water & drought (Tharaka)

The Thuci and Mutonga rivers and sand dams are the lifeline for Tharaka North and South; dry-season trekking distances there routinely exceed the highland norm. The contrast with Chuka and Maara's reliable springs is the county's starkest infrastructure gap.
Health & nutrition

GAM concentrates heavily in Tharaka's lowland wards while highland Chuka/Maara children track close to the national average. The Kiambere hydropower dam downstream benefits the national grid far more than the local Tharaka communities living beside it.

wajir.title: Wajir County
wajir.gam: 18–27% (among Kenya's highest; Tarbaj & Wajir South worst)
wajir.intro: Wajir is deep in Kenya's arid north-east, a vast expanse of semi-desert bushland straddling the Somalia border where Somali pastoral clans — Ogaden, Ajuran, Degodia and others — herd camels, cattle, sheep and goats across some of the country's harshest rangeland. Wajir town, built around its famous permanent wells, is a historic trade and administrative centre whose women's peace movement in the 1990s became a widely cited model for community-led conflict resolution across the region. Rainfall barely reaches 250mm in most years and fails outright in cyclical, worsening droughts; livestock is not just the economy but the social fabric, and its collapse in bad years drives some of Kenya's highest malnutrition and poverty rates.
wajir.subnote: Sub-county splits are indicative estimates apportioned from the 2019 county totals (781,263 people / 113,227 households); ward-level tabulation is not fully public.
sites: County HQ — historic wells, camel trade
sectors: Livestock economy

Camels are the backbone of Wajir's economy; Habaswein and Wajir town are among the largest livestock markets in northern Kenya, feeding the Garissa–Nairobi and Somalia export corridors. Recurrent drought die-offs (2017, 2022) have repeatedly wiped out large shares of herds.
Water & WASH

Households rely on shallow wells, boreholes and Wajir's traditional dug wells, locally famous for having sustained the town for generations. Dry-season trekking distances in Tarbaj and Wajir North regularly exceed 20–30km, among the longest recorded nationally.
Nutrition & health

GAM has repeatedly breached emergency thresholds in Tarbaj and Wajir South. Poor road access and dispersed settlement make health and nutrition service delivery exceptionally difficult, with mobile outreach clinics the primary model of coverage.
Conflict & governance

Clan-based resource competition — Degodia–Ajuran dynamics and cross-border tension with Somalia and Ethiopia — periodically disrupts grazing access. Wajir's women-led peace process of the 1990s remains a widely studied model for community conflict resolution in the region.

west-pokot.title: West Pokot County
west-pokot.intro: West Pokot rises from the hot, dry Suguta and Karasuk plains on the Uganda border up through the dramatic Cherangany Hills escarpment to cool, well-watered highlands around Kapenguria. The Pokot people combine cattle-and-goat pastoralism in the lowlands (Kacheliba, Alale, Pokot South) with highland maize, wheat and pyrethrum farming near Kapenguria and Sigor. Cross-border cattle raiding with Karamojong communities in Uganda, fuelled by small-arms flows, has made the northern lowlands one of Kenya's more chronically insecure pastoral belts, compounding drought vulnerability. Kapenguria's colonial-era prison, where Jomo Kenyatta was held before independence, is the county's best-known historical landmark.
subcounties: Pure pastoral — Uganda border, cattle raiding hotspot
west-pokot.subnote: Sub-county splits are indicative estimates apportioned from the 2019 county totals (621,241 people / 117,215 households); ward-level tabulation is not fully public.
sites: County HQ — highland farming, Kenyatta's colonial prison
sectors: Livestock & cross-border raiding

Cattle are central to Pokot identity and wealth. Recurrent raiding with Karamojong communities across the Uganda border around Kacheliba and Alale, fuelled by small-arms proliferation, makes security a precondition for any drought response or livelihood programme in the north.
Highland-lowland duality

Kapenguria and Sigor's highland farms — maize, wheat, pyrethrum — contrast sharply with the arid Kacheliba–Alale lowlands, giving the county one of Kenya's starkest internal development gradients within a single administrative unit.
Water & WASH

Lowland households depend on seasonal rivers such as the Suam and Wei-Wei, shallow wells and water pans. Dry-season trekking in Kacheliba and Alale routinely exceeds 10–15km for people, and considerably further for herds seeking pasture and water together.
Nutrition & education

GAM peaks in the northern lowlands during drought years, while conflict-driven school closures and pastoral mobility depress enrolment in Kacheliba and Alale relative to the more settled highland sub-counties around Kapenguria and Sigor.

turkana.title: Turkana County
turkana.gam: 20–30% (Turkana North & West historically among Kenya's highest GAM)
turkana.intro: Kenya's largest county by area and among its most arid, Turkana stretches from the jade waters of Lake Turkana — the world's largest permanent desert lake — across sun-scorched plains to the Uganda, South Sudan and Ethiopia borders. The Turkana people are overwhelmingly pastoral, herding cattle, camels, goats and sheep across rangeland that receives under 200mm of rain in most years and has suffered repeated, worsening droughts (2011, 2017, 2021–23). The county also holds globally important assets alongside its poverty: the Turkana Basin's Koobi Fora fossil sites (a cradle-of-humankind research site), the Lokichar oil find, and the still largely untapped Lotikipi aquifer. Poverty and malnutrition rates here are consistently among the highest recorded nationally.
turkana.subnote: Sub-county splits are indicative estimates apportioned from the 2019 county totals (926,976 people / 185,395 households); ward-level tabulation is not fully public.
sites: South Sudan border, former relief hub
Ethiopia border, Lake Turkana north shore
sectors: Livestock economy

Almost the entire population depends directly or indirectly on livestock. Recurrent multi-year droughts, most recently 2020–23, have killed large shares of herds county-wide, with Turkana North and West chronically worst-affected and repeat humanitarian caseloads the norm rather than the exception.
Water & WASH

The Turkwel River, boreholes and the vast but still largely untapped Lotikipi Basin aquifer, discovered in 2013, define the water landscape. Most rural households still walk long distances to unprotected sources in the dry season, and the aquifer's development remains stalled.
Nutrition & health

GAM regularly exceeds the WHO 15% emergency threshold in Turkana North and West, among the highest sustained rates in Kenya. Kakuma refugee camp adds a large additional caseload to an already stretched county health system.
Refugees, resources & conflict

Kakuma hosts one of Africa's largest refugee populations — South Sudanese, Somali, Congolese and others — reshaping the local economy through trade and aid flows. Meanwhile the Lokichar oil discovery and cross-border raiding with Pokot, Karamojong and South Sudanese groups make resource governance and peacebuilding central to county stability.
